notes.note: Law is a body of rules recognised and enforced by the State to regulate human conduct, backed by sanction. It brings order, predictability and justice, and allows people and businesses to plan with certainty. Example: company law rules on board approvals let investors know in advance how decisions will be taken.

notes.topic: schools of law (Austin, Pound, Salmond, Kelsen, Savigny, Bentham)
notes.note: Austin (analytical/imperative school) saw law as a command of the sovereign backed by sanction; Bentham (utilitarian) judged law by the greatest happiness of the greatest number; Salmond defined law as principles recognised and applied by the State in the administration of justice. Kelsen's pure theory traces every norm back to a basic norm (Grundnorm) in a hierarchy; Savigny's historical school says law grows from the spirit of the people (Volksgeist) and is found, not made; Pound's sociological school treats law as social engineering that balances competing interests.

Legislation (statutes, including delegated legislation) is the main modern source of law. Custom becomes law only if it is ancient, certain, reasonable, continuous and not opposed to statute or public policy. Precedent works through stare decisis ('stand by what is decided'): the ratio decidendi binds lower courts, obiter dicta are only persuasive, and under Article 141 of the Constitution the law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts in India.

quiz.q: A jurist argues that a municipal by-law is valid because it is authorised by a State Act, which is authorised by the Constitution, which rests on a presupposed basic norm. Whose theory is this?
options: Savigny
Pound
Bentham
Kelsen
quiz.explain: Kelsen's pure theory validates each norm through a hierarchy that ends in the Grundnorm.

quiz.q: A village practice of closing a public path to outsiders has been followed for 80 years, but the court finds it unreasonable and against public policy. The practice is:
options: Binding as an ancient custom
Binding only on villagers
Not valid law, since a custom must be reasonable and consistent with public policy
Valid until repealed by statute
quiz.explain: A custom is recognised only if, besides antiquity and continuity, it is reasonable and not opposed to law or public policy.

quiz.q: While deciding a tax case, a Supreme Court judge makes a passing remark about partnership law that was not needed to decide the case. For a High Court, this remark is:
options: Obiter dictum, of persuasive value only
Ratio decidendi, binding
Res judicata
Of no value at all
quiz.explain: Only the ratio binds under stare decisis; obiter of the Supreme Court is highly persuasive but not the ratio.

quiz.q: A District Judge disagrees with a recent Supreme Court ruling squarely on the issue before him. He must:
options: Follow it under Article 141
Refer it to the High Court for reconsideration
Follow it only if the parties agree
Ignore it if a foreign court has taken a different view
quiz.explain: Article 141 makes law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India.

quiz.q: Which thinker described law as a tool of 'social engineering' that balances individual, public and social interests?
options: Austin
Salmond
Savigny
Roscoe Pound
quiz.explain: Pound's sociological jurisprudence views law as social engineering for balancing interests.

quiz.q: A student says 'law is not made by legislators but grows out of the common consciousness of a people, like language.' This reflects:
options: Analytical school
Utilitarian school
Historical school of Savigny
Realist school
quiz.explain: Savigny's historical school locates the source of law in the Volksgeist.

desc.q: A Division Bench of a High Court is hearing a case where (i) a Supreme Court judgment directly covers the point but the Bench feels it was wrongly decided, and (ii) a Full Bench (five judges) of the same High Court has earlier taken a view on a related issue. Explain how the doctrine of precedent guides the Bench.
points: Under Article 141, the ratio of the Supreme Court judgment binds the High Court; it cannot refuse to follow it even if it thinks it is wrong.
Only the Supreme Court, through a larger bench, can overrule or reconsider its own earlier ruling; the High Court may at most note its reservations.
Within the High Court, a smaller bench is bound by the decision of a larger bench; the Division Bench must follow the Full Bench view.
If the Division Bench doubts the Full Bench view, the proper course is to refer the matter to a still larger bench through the Chief Justice, not to depart from it.
Only the ratio decidendi binds; observations in either judgment that were not necessary for the decision (obiter) are persuasive.

notes.note: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came fully into force on 26 January 1950, declaring India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. It sets up a quasi-federal, parliamentary system with a written constitution, an independent judiciary and judicial review. Under the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), Parliament's amending power under Article 368 cannot destroy core features such as rule of law, federalism or judicial review.

Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) are enforceable against the 'State' as defined in Article 12; key ones are equality (Art 14), freedoms of citizens (Art 19) and life and personal liberty (Art 21, available to all persons). Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are not enforceable in court (Art 37) but are fundamental in governance, and Fundamental Duties are in Article 51A (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976). Example: a company cannot itself claim Article 19 rights as it is not a citizen, though its shareholders may.

Articles 245-246 and the Seventh Schedule divide legislative subjects into Union, State and Concurrent Lists, with residuary power with Parliament (Art 248). On a Concurrent subject, central law prevails over a repugnant State law (Art 254(1)), unless the State law was reserved for and received the President's assent (Art 254(2)). Parliament can also legislate on State subjects in special cases, e.g., a Rajya Sabha resolution (Art 249), emergency (Art 250), request of two or more States (Art 252) or to implement treaties (Art 253).

The Supreme Court (Art 124) has writ jurisdiction (Art 32), original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes (Art 131), wide appellate power including special leave (Art 136) and advisory jurisdiction (Art 143). High Courts have writ powers under Article 226 and superintendence over subordinate courts under Article 227, while subordinate courts are governed by Articles 233-237. Independence is protected by security of tenure, removal only by a special parliamentary process and salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund.

An ordinary bill may start in either House, must pass both and then receive the President's assent (Art 111). A Money Bill (Art 110) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days. Deadlocks on ordinary bills are resolved by a joint sitting (Art 108), which is not available for Money Bills or constitutional amendments; when Parliament is not in session, the President may issue ordinances (Art 123), as Governors may under Article 213.

Article 32 (itself a fundamental right) lets a person move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, while Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose', making it wider. The five writs are habeas corpus (produce a detained person), mandamus (compel a public duty), prohibition (stop a lower court/tribunal exceeding jurisdiction), certiorari (quash an order already made without jurisdiction or in breach of natural justice) and quo warranto (question a person's right to hold a public office). Example: quo warranto lies against a person appointed to a statutory post without the required qualification.

quiz.q: A State law on a Concurrent List subject conflicts with an earlier central law. The State law was reserved for and received the President's assent. In that State:
options: The central law prevails in all cases
The State law prevails, subject to Parliament's power to amend or repeal it later
Both laws are void to the extent of conflict
The matter must go to the Supreme Court under Article 143
quiz.explain: Article 254(2) allows a State law with Presidential assent to prevail in that State, subject to the proviso enabling Parliament to override it.

quiz.q: A foreign-incorporated company in India files a writ claiming violation of the freedom to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g). The petition will most likely:
options: Succeed, as every person has Article 19 rights
Succeed only if the company is listed in India
Fail, because Article 19 rights are available only to citizens
Fail, because writs cannot be filed against the government
quiz.explain: Article 19 freedoms are guaranteed only to citizens; corporations are not citizens.

quiz.q: The Rajya Sabha wants to reject a Money Bill passed by the Lok Sabha. What is the constitutional position?
options: It can reject it outright
It can delay it for six months
It can send it to a joint sitting
It can only make recommendations within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha may ignore
quiz.explain: Article 109 limits the Rajya Sabha to recommendations within 14 days on a Money Bill.

quiz.q: A person is appointed Chairman of a statutory board without having the qualifications required by the Act. The suitable writ is:
options: Mandamus
Habeas corpus
Prohibition
Quo warranto
quiz.explain: Quo warranto tests the legal authority of a person holding a public office.

quiz.q: A foreign tourist is detained by police without any legal procedure. Can he invoke Article 21?
options: Yes, Article 21 protects every person
No, Article 21 is only for citizens
Only if his embassy consents
Only under Article 226, not Article 32
quiz.explain: Article 21 uses the word 'person', so it extends to non-citizens.

quiz.q: A joint sitting of both Houses under Article 108 CANNOT be called for which of the following?
options: An ordinary bill rejected by the Rajya Sabha
An ordinary bill on which the Houses disagree about amendments
A bill to amend the Constitution under Article 368
An ordinary bill not passed by the other House within six months
quiz.explain: Joint sittings apply only to ordinary bills; Constitution amendment bills must pass each House separately by special majority.

desc.q: A State Electricity Corporation, wholly owned by the State Government, dismisses its accounts officer for alleged misconduct without issuing any show-cause notice. Advise the officer on the constitutional remedies available.
points: The Corporation, being owned and controlled by the government and performing public functions, is an instrumentality of the 'State' under Article 12, so it is bound by Part III.
Dismissal without notice or hearing is arbitrary and breaches natural justice, violating Article 14 (and Article 21 where livelihood and reputation are affected).
He may file a writ petition under Article 226 before the High Court, or under Article 32 before the Supreme Court; Article 226 is wider and is the usual first forum.
Certiorari can quash the dismissal order and mandamus can direct reinstatement or a fresh inquiry after due hearing.
The court may decline relief if an effective statutory/service remedy exists, but this rule is discretionary and does not apply where natural justice is plainly violated.

notes.note: Interpretation is needed because statutory language may be ambiguous, broad, or silent on situations the legislature did not foresee. The primary rule is the literal rule: where the words are clear, courts give them their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result seems harsh, since judges cannot rewrite a statute. Example: if a tax law clearly taxes 'every sale', the court will not exempt a sale merely because it seems unfair.

The mischief rule from Heydon's Case (1584) asks four questions: what was the law before, what defect (mischief) it did not cover, what remedy Parliament adopted, and the true reason for that remedy; the court then reads the law to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy. The golden rule allows the court to depart from the literal meaning only so far as needed to avoid absurdity or inconsistency. Example: a ban on 'vehicles in the park' read with its purpose may not stop an ambulance answering an emergency.

Internal aids are parts of the statute itself: long title, preamble, headings, marginal notes, definition clauses, illustrations, explanations, provisos and schedules. External aids include the Statement of Objects and Reasons, committee reports, parliamentary debates (used with caution), dictionaries, earlier and later statutes, and foreign decisions. Courts use aids mainly to resolve ambiguity, not to contradict clear words.

Statutes in pari materia deal with the same subject or form part of the same system, so they are read together as one code. Meaning given to a word in one may guide its meaning in the other, and later Acts may clarify earlier ones. Example: provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita can be interpreted using settled judgments on the corresponding Code of Criminal Procedure provisions they replace.

When two provisions of the same statute appear to conflict, courts adopt the construction that gives effect to both rather than letting one nullify the other. Each provision is read in its context so the statute works as a consistent whole. Example: in Venkataramana Devaru v State of Mysore, temple-entry reform under Article 25(2)(b) was harmonised with a denomination's right to manage religious affairs under Article 26(b).

A proviso carves an exception out of, or qualifies, the main provision; it is ordinarily read together with the main enactment and does not enlarge it. It cannot be used to interpret the main section where the main section is clear, though occasionally a proviso operates as a substantive provision. It differs from an Explanation, which clarifies the meaning of the main text.

Ejusdem generis: general words following specific words of one class are limited to that class. Noscitur a sociis: a word takes colour from its associated words; expressio unius est exclusio alterius: express mention of one excludes others; generalia specialibus non derogant: a general law does not override a special law; ut res magis valeat quam pereat: prefer the reading that makes the law workable. Example: 'cars, buses, lorries and other vehicles' would not normally cover a bicycle.

The General Clauses Act 1897 supplies common definitions and rules for all Central Acts. Section 6 preserves rights, liabilities and pending proceedings on repeal unless a different intention appears; section 9 says 'from' excludes the first day and 'to' includes the last day; section 10 extends a deadline falling on a day the office is closed to the next working day. Section 13 lets the masculine include the feminine and singular include plural, and section 21 says a power to issue notifications includes the power to amend or rescind them.

quiz.q: A statute imposes a fee on 'cars, buses, lorries and other vehicles' using a city bridge. A cyclist is charged the fee. Applying the relevant maxim, the cyclist will most likely:
options: Pay, since a bicycle is literally a vehicle
Not pay, since 'other vehicles' is read as motor vehicles of the same class
Pay half the fee
Not pay, because penal statutes are always void for vagueness
quiz.explain: Ejusdem generis restricts general words to the class (motor vehicles) indicated by the specific words.

quiz.q: A notice requires objections 'from 1 March to 10 March'. Under the General Clauses Act, the period:
options: Includes both 1 and 10 March
Excludes both dates
Excludes 1 March and includes 10 March
Includes 1 March and excludes 10 March
quiz.explain: Section 9 of the General Clauses Act excludes the first day after 'from' and includes the last day with 'to'.

quiz.q: A penal Act is repealed while a prosecution under it is pending, and the repealing Act is silent. The prosecution:
options: Abates automatically
Can continue only with High Court permission
Must restart under the new Act
Continues, since repeal does not affect pending proceedings unless a different intention appears
quiz.explain: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act saves pending investigations and proceedings on repeal.

quiz.q: A literal reading of a provision would require a person to file a return before the tax year even begins, an obviously absurd result. The court will most likely apply:
options: Golden rule
Rule of strict construction against the taxpayer
Ejusdem generis
Expressio unius
quiz.explain: The golden rule permits modifying the literal meaning to avoid absurdity.

quiz.q: A special Act on cooperative banks gives a specific procedure for recovery; a later general Act gives a different procedure for 'all banks'. Which applies to cooperative banks?
options: The later general Act, as later law prevails
Neither, the conflict voids both
Both, at the creditor's choice
The special Act, unless the general Act clearly shows intent to override it
quiz.explain: Generalia specialibus non derogant: a general law does not ordinarily override a special one.

quiz.q: A section grants a deduction to 'all companies', followed by a proviso 'provided that this shall not apply to banking companies'. The proviso:
options: Enlarges the main section to cover non-companies
Is to be ignored if inconsistent
Qualifies the main provision by excepting banking companies
Is merely an explanation
quiz.explain: A proviso carves out an exception from the main enactment it is attached to.

desc.q: A State notification exempts 'hospitals, nursing homes, dispensaries and other institutions' from a property cess. A private fitness centre claims the exemption as an 'other institution'. Using rules of interpretation, advise whether its claim is sustainable.
points: Under ejusdem generis, the general words 'other institutions' take their meaning from the preceding specific words, which form a genus of medical/health-care institutions.
Noscitur a sociis supports the same result: the phrase is coloured by its neighbouring words.
The mischief/purpose behind the exemption is to support provision of medical care; a commercial fitness centre does not advance that purpose.
Exemption provisions are construed strictly, and the burden is on the claimant to show it clearly falls within the exemption; any doubt goes in favour of the revenue.
Conclusion: the fitness centre's claim is unlikely to succeed.

notes.note: Administrative law governs the powers and procedures of administrative authorities and the remedies of persons affected by their actions. It grew with the welfare state, as the executive took on delegated legislation, licensing, regulation and adjudication through tribunals. India has no single code; its sources are the Constitution, statutes, delegated legislation, and above all judicial decisions. Example: SEBI's rule-making and adjudication powers are controlled by these principles.

Natural justice has two core rules: nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in his own cause, covering pecuniary, personal and official bias) and audi alteram partem (hear the other side, which requires notice, disclosure of material and a fair opportunity to respond). Courts also expect reasoned orders. After Maneka Gandhi (1978) fair procedure is linked to Articles 14 and 21; exceptions include genuine urgency (with a post-decisional hearing), statutory exclusion and purely legislative acts.

Administrative discretion is the power to choose between courses of action within legal limits. It is abused when exercised mala fide, for an improper purpose, on irrelevant considerations, under dictation of another authority, or so unreasonably that no sensible authority would do it (Wednesbury unreasonableness); failure to exercise it, such as fettering it by rigid policy or non-application of mind, is also illegal. Courts increasingly test discretion affecting rights on proportionality.

Judicial review lets constitutional courts examine the legality of administrative action under Articles 32, 226 and 227, and it is part of the basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997). The broad grounds are illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety (Lord Diplock's GCHQ formulation), with proportionality as an emerging ground. The court reviews the decision-making process, not the merits, and does not substitute its own decision.

Under Article 300 the Union and States can sue and be sued. In tort, older cases distinguished sovereign functions (immune, Kasturi Lal, 1965) from non-sovereign functions (liable, State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati, 1962), but for violations of Article 21 courts award public-law compensation where sovereign immunity is no defence (Rudul Sah, 1983; Nilabati Behera, 1993). Government contracts must comply with Article 299 (expressed in the name of the President/Governor and executed by an authorised person); non-compliant contracts are unenforceable, but restitution may be claimed under section 70 of the Indian Contract Act.

quiz.q: A member of a selection board participates in interviews where his nephew is a candidate, though he does not mark his nephew. The selection is likely to be:
options: Vitiated by bias, since a reasonable likelihood of bias is enough
Valid, as he did not mark his nephew
Valid if other members agreed
Invalid only if the nephew is selected first
quiz.explain: The rule against bias (nemo judex) is breached where a real likelihood of bias exists; actual bias need not be proved.

quiz.q: A licensing officer cancels a licence solely because the Minister phoned and told him to, without examining the file. The action is bad because:
options: The officer acted under dictation and failed to exercise his own discretion
Ministers cannot frame policy
Licences can never be cancelled
No appeal was provided
quiz.explain: Discretion vested in an authority must be exercised by that authority; acting under dictation is an abuse of discretion.

quiz.q: A contractor supplied goods to a State department under an oral arrangement not complying with Article 299. The State used the goods but refuses to pay. The contractor can:
options: Enforce the contract fully
Claim nothing
Claim compensation for the benefit enjoyed under section 70 of the Indian Contract Act
Only file a writ of habeas corpus
quiz.explain: A contract violating Article 299 is unenforceable, but section 70 allows restitution for non-gratuitous benefits enjoyed.

quiz.q: A person dies in police custody due to torture. In a writ petition, the State argues sovereign immunity. The court will most likely:
options: Accept the plea, as policing is a sovereign function
Direct the family to file a civil suit only
Dismiss the petition for want of jurisdiction
Award compensation, as sovereign immunity is no defence to Article 21 violations in public law
quiz.explain: Nilabati Behera recognised strict public-law liability for violation of Article 21.

quiz.q: In judicial review of a tender decision, the High Court will ordinarily examine:
options: Whether it would have chosen a better bidder
The fairness, legality and rationality of the decision-making process
The commercial merits of each bid in detail
Only the price quoted
quiz.explain: Judicial review is concerned with the decision-making process, not the merits.

quiz.q: In which situation may a prior hearing be lawfully dispensed with?
options: When the officer is busy
When the affected person is a company
When food stocks are found spreading a dangerous infection and must be seized at once, with a hearing given afterwards
Whenever the statute is silent about hearing
quiz.explain: Urgency in public interest can justify excluding a prior hearing, usually with a post-decisional hearing.

desc.q: A municipal officer demolishes part of a trader's shop overnight claiming it encroaches on a public road, without issuing any notice. The trader alleges the officer has a personal grudge against him. Discuss the legality of the action and the trader's remedies.
points: Demolition affects property and livelihood, so audi alteram partem requires prior notice and a fair chance to respond; no genuine emergency is shown.
If personal enmity is established, the action is vitiated by bias and mala fides, an abuse of discretion.
The trader may file a writ under Article 226 seeking certiorari to quash the action and mandamus to restrain further action without due process.
The court may award compensation in public law for arbitrary deprivation, besides any civil remedy for damages.
Even if an encroachment exists, the authority must follow the procedure prescribed by the municipal statute; the remedy is a fresh decision after hearing.

notes.note: A tort is a civil wrong, other than breach of contract or trust, remedied by unliquidated damages. Liability needs a wrongful act or omission by the defendant, legal damage (violation of a legal right) to the plaintiff, and a legal remedy. Violation of a legal right is actionable even without actual loss (injuria sine damno, Ashby v White), while actual loss without violation of a legal right is not (damnum sine injuria, Gloucester Grammar School case); example: a rival opening a cheaper shop next door causes loss but no tort.

Under strict liability (Rylands v Fletcher, 1868), a person who brings a dangerous thing onto land for non-natural use is liable if it escapes and causes harm, even without negligence, subject to defences such as act of God, plaintiff's own fault, consent, act of a stranger and statutory authority. In M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1987, oleum gas leak), the Supreme Court laid down absolute liability for hazardous or inherently dangerous industries with no such exceptions, and damages linked to the enterprise's capacity. The Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 requires such units to carry insurance for immediate relief.

A person may be liable for a tort committed by another because of their relationship, mainly master and servant, principal and agent, and partners. An employer is liable for torts of an employee in the course of employment, including an unauthorised or wrongful way of doing an authorised act (Lloyd v Grace Smith & Co, fraud by a clerk), but not for acts on a 'frolic of his own'. An employer is generally not liable for an independent contractor, except for non-delegable duties or hazardous work.

A company, as a legal person, is liable in tort for wrongs committed by its employees and agents in the course of its business, just like a natural employer. For crimes, courts attribute the mental state of its 'directing mind and will' to it (Iridium India Telecom, 2010), and a company can be prosecuted even for offences carrying mandatory imprisonment, by imposing a fine (Standard Chartered Bank v Directorate of Enforcement, 2005). Example: a company is liable for a delivery van accident caused by its driver on duty.

Judicial remedies are damages (nominal, contemptuous, compensatory or exemplary to punish outrageous conduct), injunctions (temporary, permanent, prohibitory or mandatory) and specific restitution of property. Extra-judicial remedies include self-defence, expulsion of a trespasser, re-entry on land, recaption of goods, abatement of nuisance and distress damage feasant. Example: a factory emitting fumes may be restrained by injunction and made to pay damages to neighbours.

quiz.q: A returning officer wrongfully refuses to let Ravi vote; Ravi's candidate wins anyway. Ravi sues. The court will most likely:
options: Dismiss the suit as Ravi suffered no loss
Hold the State liable but not the officer
Refer it to the Election Commission only
Hold the officer liable since Ravi's legal right was violated
quiz.explain: Injuria sine damno: violation of a legal right is actionable without proof of loss (Ashby v White).

quiz.q: A new coaching centre opens opposite an established one, charges lower fees and draws away students. The established centre:
options: Can recover damages for loss of profits
Can get an injunction
Has no remedy, because loss without infringement of a legal right is not actionable
Can sue for nuisance
quiz.explain: Damnum sine injuria: honest competition causing loss is not a tort.

quiz.q: Toxic gas leaks from a chemical plant and injures residents. The company proves it took all reasonable care and that the leak resulted from sabotage by an outsider. The company is:
options: Not liable, due to act of a stranger
Liable only if negligence is proved
Liable only to the extent of its insurance
Liable under the rule of absolute liability, with no exceptions
quiz.explain: M.C. Mehta absolute liability for hazardous industries admits no exception such as act of a stranger.

quiz.q: A clerk of a property firm, acting within his apparent authority, induces a client to transfer property to him and then sells it for himself. The firm is:
options: Liable, because the fraud was committed in the course of employment
Not liable, as the firm gained nothing
Not liable, as fraud is always outside employment
Liable only if partners knew
quiz.explain: Lloyd v Grace Smith: an employer is liable for an employee's fraud committed in the course of employment, even for the employee's own benefit.

quiz.q: Water from a factory reservoir escapes after an unprecedented cloudburst and floods a neighbour's farm. Under Rylands v Fletcher, the factory can best plead:
options: Act of God
Volenti non fit injuria
Statutory authority
Contributory negligence
quiz.explain: Act of God (an extraordinary natural event) is a defence to strict liability.

quiz.q: A court awards damages far above the actual loss to mark its disapproval of a defendant's deliberate and oppressive conduct. These are:
options: Nominal damages
Contemptuous damages
Exemplary damages
Prospective damages
quiz.explain: Exemplary (punitive) damages punish and deter outrageous conduct.

desc.q: A courier company's driver, while on his delivery route, drives fast to finish early and injures a pedestrian. Later the same day, he takes the van 20 km off route to attend a friend's party and injures a cyclist. Discuss the company's liability.
points: An employer is vicariously liable for torts of its employee committed in the course of employment.
Speeding on the delivery route is a wrongful mode of doing an authorised act (delivery), so the company is liable for the pedestrian's injury.
The detour for a personal party is a 'frolic of his own', outside the course of employment, so the company is ordinarily not liable for the cyclist's injury.
The driver is personally liable in both cases, jointly with the company in the first case.
Victims may claim compensation (including through motor accident claims) with damages assessed for injury, medical cost and loss of income.

notes.note: Under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC), civil courts can try all suits of a civil nature unless their cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred, e.g., matters reserved to tribunals or the DRT. Jurisdiction depends on pecuniary value, territory and subject matter; section 15 requires a suit to be filed in the lowest competent court. Sections 16-20 decide the place of suing: immovable property suits where the property lies, and others where the defendant resides or carries on business or where the cause of action arose.

A judgment (section 2(9)) is the statement of the grounds on which the judge bases a decree or order. A decree (section 2(2)) is the formal expression of an adjudication that conclusively determines the rights of the parties on matters in controversy; it may be preliminary, final or partly both, and includes rejection of a plaint. An order (section 2(14)) is any formal decision of a civil court that is not a decree; example: granting a temporary injunction is an order, while a decree for possession finally settles the right.

Section 11 CPC bars a court from trying a matter directly and substantially in issue in an earlier suit between the same parties (or those claiming under them), litigating under the same title, which a competent court has heard and finally decided. Constructive res judicata (Explanation IV) covers grounds that might and ought to have been raised earlier. It differs from res sub judice under section 10, which only stays a later suit while the earlier one on the same matter is pending.

First appeals from original decrees lie under section 96, and second appeals to the High Court under section 100 only on a substantial question of law; appeals from specified orders lie under section 104 and Order XLIII. Review under section 114 and Order XLVII is by the same court for discovery of new evidence, an error apparent on the record or another sufficient reason. Revision under section 115 lets the High Court correct jurisdictional errors of subordinate courts in cases where no appeal lies.

Under section 26 and Order VII, a suit is instituted by presenting a plaint containing the parties' details, facts constituting the cause of action, jurisdiction and relief claimed. Under Order VII Rule 11, a plaint is rejected if it discloses no cause of action, is undervalued or insufficiently stamped and not corrected, or is barred by law. Section 80 requires two months' notice before suing the government or a public officer, though urgent relief may be sought with leave of the court.

The Commercial Courts Act 2015 sets up Commercial Courts, Commercial Divisions of High Courts and Commercial Appellate Courts/Divisions for commercial disputes of a specified value of ₹3 lakh or more. Under section 12A, a suit that does not seek urgent interim relief must first go through pre-institution mediation (held mandatory in Patil Automation, 2022). It also amends the CPC for such suits with strict timelines for written statements, case management hearings and summary judgment; example: a dispute over unpaid invoices of ₹10 lakh between two traders is a commercial dispute.

quiz.q: A suit for possession of land in Pune is filed in a Mumbai court because the defendant lives in Mumbai. The court should:
options: Try it, as the defendant resides there
Return the plaint for presentation to the Pune court, where the property lies
Transfer it to the Supreme Court
Try it only with the defendant's consent
quiz.explain: Section 16 CPC requires suits relating to immovable property to be filed where the property is situated.

quiz.q: A tenant loses an eviction suit. In a fresh suit against the same landlord over the same premises, he raises a defence he could have raised earlier but didn't. The court will:
options: Hear the new defence on merits
Allow it only on payment of costs
Bar it as constructive res judicata
Stay the suit under section 10
quiz.explain: Explanation IV to section 11 treats matters that might and ought to have been raised as having been decided.

quiz.q: A party wants the High Court to hear a second appeal on a pure question of fact. The appeal:
options: Is maintainable as of right
Is maintainable if the value exceeds ₹5 lakh
Is not maintainable, since section 100 requires a substantial question of law
Must be filed in the Supreme Court
quiz.explain: Section 100 CPC limits second appeals to cases involving a substantial question of law.

quiz.q: A supplier sues a buyer for ₹12 lakh due on goods under a commercial contract, seeking no urgent interim relief. Before filing, the supplier must:
options: Send a section 80 notice
Obtain High Court leave
Deposit 25% of the claim
Exhaust pre-institution mediation under section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act
quiz.explain: Section 12A makes pre-institution mediation mandatory for commercial suits not seeking urgent interim relief.

quiz.q: Shortly after the decree, a litigant discovers a registered document that, despite due diligence, he could not find earlier and which goes to the root of the case. The appropriate remedy before the same court is:
options: Review
Revision
Second appeal
Reference
quiz.explain: Order XLVII permits review on discovery of new and important evidence not available despite due diligence.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a 'decree' under the CPC?
options: An order granting a temporary injunction
An order dismissing a suit for default of appearance
An order adjourning the hearing
Rejection of a plaint
quiz.explain: Section 2(2) expressly includes rejection of a plaint, while dismissal for default is excluded.

desc.q: X files a suit against Y for recovery of ₹8 lakh in a Delhi civil court. During its pendency, X files a second suit against Y in a Gurugram court on the same cause. Later the Delhi suit is decided against X on merits. Advise Y on the procedural defences available.
points: While the Delhi suit was pending, Y could seek a stay of the later Gurugram suit under section 10 CPC (res sub judice), since the matter in issue is directly and substantially the same between the same parties.
Once the Delhi court, being competent, decided the suit on merits, Y can plead res judicata under section 11 in the Gurugram suit.
Conditions are met: same parties, same matter in issue, same title, competent court and final decision on merits.
Y may also seek rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 or dismissal, and claim costs for vexatious litigation.
X's proper remedy against the Delhi decree is a first appeal under section 96, not a parallel suit.

notes.note: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024, provides for the High Court, Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the First and Second Class, and Executive Magistrates. The BNSS dropped the separate category of Metropolitan Magistrates, and the Chief Judicial Magistrate heads the magistracy in each district. A Sessions Judge can pass any sentence authorised by law, but a death sentence must be confirmed by the High Court.

Police may arrest without warrant in cognizable cases on the grounds in section 35 BNSS (old CrPC section 41), but for offences punishable up to seven years they must be satisfied that arrest is necessary; otherwise a notice of appearance is issued (Arnesh Kumar, 2014). The arrested person must be told the grounds and his right to bail, may meet an advocate, must have a relative or friend informed, and must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (also Article 22). Private persons may arrest someone committing a non-bailable and cognizable offence in their presence or a proclaimed offender.

A crime generally needs both actus reus (a guilty act or omission) and mens rea (a guilty mind such as intention, knowledge or negligence), captured in the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea. Some regulatory and public-welfare offences are of strict liability, where mens rea need not be proved. Example: a person who takes another's umbrella honestly believing it to be his own lacks the dishonest intention needed for theft.

A cognizable offence is one where police may arrest without warrant and investigate without a Magistrate's order; in non-cognizable cases police need a Magistrate's order to investigate. The First Schedule of the BNSS classifies offences as cognizable or not, bailable or not. The BNSS (section 173) also allows information to be given electronically (e-FIR) and recognises 'zero FIR' registration irrespective of jurisdiction, with a preliminary inquiry option for certain offences punishable from three to seven years.

In bailable offences bail is a matter of right; in non-bailable offences it is the court's discretion based on the gravity of the offence, the risk of absconding and the risk of tampering with evidence. The BNSS provides for anticipatory bail (section 482, old CrPC 438) and default bail if the investigation is not completed in time. An undertrial who has spent half the maximum sentence (one-third for first-time offenders) is to be released on bail under section 479 BNSS (old CrPC 436A).

A summons is a court's order to appear, served personally or by other modes, and the BNSS now allows electronic service. A warrant of arrest is a written order directing police to arrest and produce a person; it may be bailable (with an endorsement for release on bond) and remains in force until cancelled or executed. If a person absconds, the court may issue a proclamation requiring appearance and attach his property; in summons cases a summons is usually issued first, while warrants are used in serious cases.

Criminal breach of trust under section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS; old IPC section 405) is committed when a person entrusted with property dishonestly misappropriates it or uses or disposes of it against the terms of the trust. Entrustment is the key element and distinguishes it from theft; higher punishment applies to carriers, clerks, servants, bankers, agents and public servants. Example: a company director who uses the company's escrow funds for personal debts commits criminal breach of trust.

Cheating under section 318 BNS (old IPC sections 415/420) means deceiving a person to fraudulently or dishonestly induce him to deliver property, or to do or omit something he would not otherwise do, causing or likely to cause harm. The dishonest intention must exist at the time of the inducement; a mere later failure to keep a promise is a civil breach, not cheating. Example: issuing fake shipping documents to obtain an advance payment is cheating.

Forgery under section 336 BNS (old IPC section 463) is making a false document or electronic record with intent to cause damage or injury, support a claim, cause a person to part with property or commit fraud. A 'false document' (section 335 BNS, old IPC 464) includes one made or altered dishonestly so it appears to be made by someone who did not make it, including affixing another's electronic signature. Using a forged document as genuine is a separate offence (section 340 BNS, old IPC 471).

Defamation under section 356 BNS (old IPC sections 499/500) is making or publishing an imputation, by words, signs or visible representation, intending or knowing it will harm a person's reputation; companies and associations can also be defamed. Exceptions include true statements made for the public good, fair comment on public conduct, fair reports of court proceedings and good-faith complaints to authorities. The BNS adds community service as a possible punishment, and the offence remains non-cognizable, prosecuted on the complaint of the aggrieved person.

quiz.q: Police arrest a person at 10 a.m. on Monday for a cognizable offence. The latest by which he must be produced before a Magistrate (excluding travel time) is:
options: 10 a.m. Tuesday
10 a.m. Wednesday
Within 48 hours
Whenever the investigation is complete
quiz.explain: Section 58 BNSS (old CrPC 57) and Article 22(2) require production within 24 hours.

quiz.q: A shop employee is given cash daily to deposit in the bank. One day he spends it on himself. The offence is:
options: Theft
Cheating
Criminal breach of trust
Forgery
quiz.explain: Dishonest misappropriation of property entrusted to him is criminal breach of trust under section 316 BNS.

quiz.q: A borrower takes a loan genuinely intending to repay but later defaults due to business losses. The lender files a criminal complaint for cheating. The complaint will likely fail because:
options: Dishonest intention at the time of inducement is absent
Loans are never covered by criminal law
Cheating requires a forged document
Only banks can complain
quiz.explain: Cheating under section 318 BNS requires fraudulent or dishonest intention at the inception.

quiz.q: For an offence punishable with up to five years, police want to arrest the accused who is cooperating and has a fixed address. The police should ordinarily:
options: Arrest immediately
Seek a warrant from the Sessions Court
Arrest only after charge-sheet
Issue a notice of appearance unless arrest is shown to be necessary
quiz.explain: Section 35 BNSS and Arnesh Kumar require recorded necessity for arrest in offences up to seven years, otherwise a notice of appearance.

quiz.q: An accountant scans his manager's signature onto a letter authorising a payment to himself. He has committed:
options: Forgery, by making a false document with intent to commit fraud
Only cheating
Defamation
No offence, since no ink signature was copied
quiz.explain: Making a false document or electronic record with intent to defraud is forgery under section 336 BNS.

quiz.q: A newspaper publishes an accurate report of court proceedings in a fraud trial, showing a businessman in poor light. He sues for criminal defamation. The newspaper can rely on:
options: No defence; any harm to reputation is defamation
The defence of consent
The exception for publication of substantially true reports of court proceedings
Sovereign immunity
quiz.explain: Section 356 BNS protects substantially true reports of the proceedings of courts.

desc.q: Mr. A, Managing Director of a private company, receives ₹50 lakh from investors for a specific project, diverts the money to repay his personal loan, and produces a fabricated board resolution to show the diversion was approved. Identify the offences involved under the new criminal laws and comment on the procedural position.
points: Money received for a specific purpose and diverted is criminal breach of trust under section 316 BNS (old IPC 405/409); as a director/agent he may face the aggravated form.
Producing a fabricated board resolution is making a false document (sections 335-336 BNS, old IPC 463-464) and using it as genuine (section 340 BNS, old IPC 471).
If the investors were induced to pay through false representations made with dishonest intent from the start, cheating under section 318 BNS (old IPC 420) is also attracted.
These are cognizable offences; an FIR can be lodged under section 173 BNSS (including e-FIR) and police can investigate without a Magistrate's order.
A may apply for anticipatory bail under section 482 BNSS; the company and investors can also pursue civil recovery and corporate-law remedies.

notes.note: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) replaced the Indian Evidence Act 1872 from 1 July 2024, largely keeping its structure. Relevancy is a matter of logic: a fact is relevant if it is connected with the fact in issue as provided in the Act (e.g., res gestae, motive, preparation, conduct). Admissibility is a matter of law: a relevant fact may still be excluded, such as a confession made to a police officer, which is inadmissible under the BSA (old section 25).

Some facts need no proof: facts judicially noticed by the court (such as laws in force, national holidays and the territories of India) and facts admitted by the parties. All other facts in issue and relevant facts must be proved by evidence. 'Proved' means the court believes the fact exists or considers its existence so probable that a prudent person would act on it; in criminal cases the standard is proof beyond reasonable doubt.

Opinions of experts in foreign law, science, art, handwriting and finger impressions are relevant, and the BSA expressly adds the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence under section 79A of the IT Act (old Evidence Act sections 45 and 45A). Expert opinion is advisory: the court weighs the reasons given and is not bound by it. Example: a handwriting expert's opinion on a disputed signature on a cheque is corroborative evidence.

Oral evidence must be direct: the person who saw, heard or perceived the fact must testify, and hearsay is generally excluded. Documentary evidence is proved by primary evidence (the document itself) and, in specified cases, by secondary evidence such as certified copies, with the BSA treating electronic and digital records as documents and widening secondary evidence to include oral and written admissions and expert-examined copies. Circumstantial evidence can found a conviction if the chain of circumstances is complete and consistent only with guilt (Sharad Birdhichand Sarda, 1984).

Whoever asserts a fact must prove it (old Evidence Act sections 101-103), and the burden of proving facts that bring a person within an exception, such as self-defence, lies on that person (old section 105). Facts especially within a person's knowledge must be proved by him (old section 106), and courts may draw presumptions, such as a dowry death presumption. Example: a company claiming a payment was a loan, not income, must prove the loan.

Estoppel (old section 115 of the Evidence Act) prevents a person who by declaration, act or omission has made another believe a thing and act on that belief from later denying it. A tenant is estopped from denying the landlord's title during the tenancy, and a licensee from denying the licensor's title. Promissory estoppel can bind even the government where a party has altered its position on a promise, but there is no estoppel against a statute.

Under the BSA, electronic records are primary evidence when produced as the original record, including records stored in multiple files or automatically, and secondary copies are admissible with a certificate (old section 65B of the Evidence Act). The BSA prescribes a certificate in the Schedule signed by the person in charge of the device and by an expert. The Supreme Court in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) held the certificate mandatory for secondary electronic evidence; example: WhatsApp chats produced as screenshots need the certificate.

quiz.q: An accused makes a confession to a Sub-Inspector during interrogation, and the prosecution seeks to prove it at trial. The confession is:
options: Admissible as an admission
Admissible if voluntary
Admissible only if recorded on video
Inadmissible, since confessions to police officers cannot be proved against the accused
quiz.explain: The BSA, like old Evidence Act section 25, bars proof of confessions made to a police officer.

quiz.q: A company wants to prove emails printed from its server. To make these printouts admissible as secondary evidence, it must generally produce:
options: An affidavit of the CEO only
The certificate required under the BSA (old section 65B)
Testimony of the email recipient only
Nothing; printouts are always primary evidence
quiz.explain: Secondary electronic evidence requires the prescribed certificate (Arjun Panditrao Khotkar).

quiz.q: An accused pleads private defence in a murder trial. The burden to prove circumstances bringing the case within that exception lies on:
options: The accused, on a preponderance of probabilities
The prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt
The court
The investigating officer
quiz.explain: The person claiming a general exception must prove it (old section 105), though on the lower civil standard.

quiz.q: A tenant who has paid rent to L for years refuses to pay, claiming L never owned the property. During the tenancy the tenant:
options: Can deny L's title freely
Can deny title only with court permission
Must pay rent to the government
Is estopped from denying L's title
quiz.explain: Tenant estoppel prevents a tenant from denying the landlord's title during the tenancy.

quiz.q: The prosecution case rests entirely on circumstantial evidence. A conviction is safe only if:
options: At least one eyewitness corroborates
The accused fails to testify
The circumstances form a complete chain pointing only to the accused's guilt
Motive is proved
quiz.explain: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda requires a complete chain consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt.

quiz.q: Which of the following does NOT need to be proved by evidence?
options: The existence of a statute in force in India
The date a contract was signed
The contents of a private letter
The quality of goods supplied
quiz.explain: Courts take judicial notice of laws in force, so they need not be proved.

desc.q: In a cheque-fraud trial, the prosecution relies on (i) a handwriting expert's report on the signature, (ii) CCTV footage copied onto a pen drive from the bank's system, and (iii) a statement the accused made to the bank manager admitting the act. Comment on the evidentiary value of each under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023.
points: The handwriting expert's opinion is relevant expert evidence, but it is advisory; the court will look for corroboration and the reasons behind the opinion.

The pen-drive copy of CCTV footage is secondary electronic evidence and needs the prescribed certificate (old section 65B equivalent) for admissibility; the original system record would be primary evidence.
A confession to a bank manager, not a police officer, is not barred as a police confession; it is admissible if voluntary and not caused by inducement, threat or promise.
The court will weigh all three pieces together; any confession is used with corroboration.
The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; gaps such as a missing certificate can make the CCTV footage inadmissible.

notes.note: Under the Specific Relief Act 1963, as amended in 2018, specific performance of a contract is no longer discretionary: section 10 says it 'shall' be enforced, subject to sections 11(2), 14 and 16. Section 14 lists contracts that cannot be specifically enforced, e.g., where the party has obtained substituted performance under section 20, contracts involving continuous supervision, those dependent on personal qualifications, and determinable contracts. Section 16 bars relief to a party who has not performed or been ready and willing to perform his essential obligations.

Under section 27, a party may sue to rescind a contract that is voidable or terminable by him, or unlawful for reasons not apparent on its face where the defendant is more to blame. Rescission is refused if the plaintiff has ratified the contract, the parties cannot be restored to their original position, or third parties have acquired rights in good faith and for value. Example: a buyer induced by fraud to buy a flat may seek rescission if he acts before ratifying.

Under section 31, a person who reasonably fears serious injury from a void or voidable written instrument may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable and cancelled. If the instrument is registered, the court sends a copy of the decree to the registering officer to note the cancellation. Partial cancellation is allowed under section 32; example: a forged sale deed registered in someone else's name can be cancelled.

Section 34 allows a person entitled to a legal character or a right to property to sue for a declaration of that status or right against a person denying it. The court will not grant a mere declaration where the plaintiff could seek further relief (such as possession) but omits to do so. Under section 35, the declaration binds only the parties and persons claiming through them; example: a declaration that the plaintiff is the lawful owner of shares.

Preventive relief is granted by injunctions: temporary injunctions are regulated by the CPC (Order XXXIX), while perpetual injunctions are granted by decree under sections 37-38 to prevent breach of an obligation. Mandatory injunctions under section 39 compel a positive act, such as removing an illegal construction. Section 41 lists cases where injunction is refused, and after 2018 it bars injunctions that would impede or delay infrastructure projects (clause (ha)).

quiz.q: After the 2018 amendment, a buyer who has paid the full price and stands ready to take delivery seeks specific performance of a land sale agreement. The court:
options: May refuse at its discretion if damages are adequate
Must decree specific performance unless a statutory bar applies
Can grant only compensation
Must refer the matter to mediation
quiz.explain: Section 10 as amended makes specific performance the rule, subject to sections 11(2), 14 and 16.

quiz.q: A party seeks specific performance of a contract to have a famous singer perform at a wedding. Relief will be refused because:
options: The contract depends on personal qualifications of a party
Wedding contracts are void
Only damages up to ₹1 lakh are available
Specific performance is never granted for services
quiz.explain: Section 14 bars specific enforcement of contracts that depend on personal qualifications.

quiz.q: A plaintiff seeks only a declaration that he owns a shop, although the defendant is in possession and the plaintiff could have claimed possession. The court will:
options: Grant the declaration
Grant possession on its own
Refuse the declaration under the proviso to section 34
Transfer the case to revenue authorities
quiz.explain: The proviso to section 34 bars a mere declaration where further relief was available but not sought.

quiz.q: Someone has had a forged gift deed of A's house registered. A's appropriate relief is:
options: Rescission under section 27
Specific performance
Declaration only
Cancellation of the instrument under section 31
quiz.explain: Section 31 allows cancellation of a void instrument likely to cause serious injury.

quiz.q: A neighbour has built a wall blocking A's established right of way. A seeks an order requiring the neighbour to demolish the wall. This relief is:
options: A prohibitory injunction
Rescission
A declaratory decree
A mandatory injunction under section 39
quiz.explain: Section 39 allows mandatory injunctions compelling performance of acts needed to prevent breach of an obligation.

quiz.q: A buyer induced by misrepresentation to buy machinery keeps using it for a year after learning the truth, then seeks rescission. The court will likely:
options: Grant rescission as of right
Grant rescission with interest
Refuse rescission because he has ratified the contract
Grant specific performance instead
quiz.explain: Section 27(2) bars rescission where the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract.

desc.q: A agreed to sell his flat to B for ₹80 lakh. B paid ₹20 lakh as advance and has kept the balance ready, but A now refuses to execute the sale deed because prices have risen. A argues that B can be compensated with damages. Advise B in light of the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2018.
points: After 2018, section 10 makes specific performance mandatory, subject only to sections 11(2), 14 and 16; adequacy of damages is no longer a ground for refusal.
A sale of a specific flat is not covered by any section 14 bar.
B must prove readiness and willingness to perform under section 16(c), e.g., by showing availability of the balance funds throughout.
B should sue within three years from the date fixed for performance, or from when refusal was notified (Limitation Act, Article 54).
B may also seek a temporary injunction restraining A from selling the flat to anyone else during the suit, and may claim compensation in addition under section 21.

notes.note: The Limitation Act 1963 prescribes periods in its Schedule (e.g., three years for most contract-based money suits). Under section 12, the day from which the period runs is excluded, and time needed to obtain copies of the decree or order is excluded for appeals. Section 14 excludes time spent prosecuting in good faith in a court without jurisdiction, and section 15 excludes periods of stay or notice; under section 4, if the period ends on a court holiday, the case may be filed on reopening.

Section 3 makes every suit, appeal or application filed after the prescribed period liable to be dismissed, even if limitation is not raised as a defence. Limitation bars the remedy, not the right: a time-barred debt still exists and can be paid or set off, and a time-barred debt can support a fresh promise under section 25(3) of the Contract Act. Under section 5, appeals and applications (but not suits) may be admitted late if the applicant shows sufficient cause, which courts construe liberally.

Under section 18, a written and signed acknowledgment of liability made before the period expires gives a fresh period of limitation from the date of acknowledgment. It need not specify the exact amount and may be made by the debtor or his authorised agent. Section 19 gives a similar fresh start from the date of part-payment of debt or interest, provided it is made before expiry; example: a balance confirmation signed by a company in its audited accounts can operate as acknowledgment.

Under section 27, when the period for a suit for possession of property expires, the owner's right to the property itself is extinguished, an exception to the rule that limitation bars only the remedy. A person in open, continuous, hostile possession for 12 years (30 years against the government) can thus acquire title by adverse possession, under Articles 65 and 112. In Ravinder Kaur Grewal (2019), the Supreme Court held that such a person can also sue as plaintiff to protect that title.

quiz.q: A debt of ₹5 lakh fell due on 1 April 2022. On 15 March 2025, the debtor signs a letter admitting he owes the amount. The creditor can now sue up to:
options: 31 March 2025
1 April 2026
15 March 2028
There is no limit
quiz.explain: Section 18 gives a fresh three-year period from the date of written acknowledgment made within the original period.

quiz.q: A plaintiff files a money suit 40 days late and asks the court to condone the delay under section 5 citing illness. The court:
options: Cannot condone, as section 5 does not apply to suits
Must condone if illness is proved
May condone if sufficient cause is shown
Must refer to the High Court
quiz.explain: Section 5 extends only to appeals and applications, not suits.

quiz.q: A company's debt became time-barred in 2023. In 2025 the debtor voluntarily pays it. Later he sues to recover the payment as not legally due. He will:
options: Succeed, since limitation extinguished the debt
Succeed with interest
Fail, since limitation bars only the remedy and not the debt itself
Succeed only for half the amount
quiz.explain: Limitation bars the remedy, not the right; a time-barred debt paid voluntarily cannot be recovered.

quiz.q: A has occupied B's private land openly, continuously and hostilely for 13 years. B now sues for possession. The likely result is:
options: B succeeds, as ownership never lapses
B succeeds if he shows title documents
The suit is referred to arbitration
B's suit is time-barred and his title is extinguished under section 27
quiz.explain: The 12-year period for possession based on title runs against B, and section 27 extinguishes his right.

quiz.q: A party files a suit in good faith in a court that lacks jurisdiction and, after the plaint is returned, refiles in the correct court. While computing limitation, the time spent in the wrong court:
options: Is excluded under section 14
Is included in full
Is excluded only if the defendant agrees
Is excluded only for appeals
quiz.explain: Section 14 excludes time spent in bona fide proceedings in a court without jurisdiction.

quiz.q: A debtor makes a part-payment of interest after the limitation period has expired. This:
options: Revives the debt with a fresh period
Has no effect on limitation, since section 19 requires payment before expiry
Extends limitation by one year
Converts the debt into a decree
quiz.explain: Section 19 applies only to payments made before the expiry of the prescribed period.

desc.q: ABC Ltd supplied goods to XYZ Ltd; the invoice of ₹15 lakh fell due on 10 June 2021. XYZ paid ₹2 lakh on 5 May 2024 and emailed a balance confirmation on 1 August 2024. ABC Ltd now wishes to sue in December 2026. Advise on limitation.
points: A suit for price of goods sold has a three-year period, running from the due date (10 June 2021), so it would expire on 10 June 2024.
Part-payment of ₹2 lakh on 5 May 2024 was within the period, so under section 19 a fresh three-year period runs from 5 May 2024, i.e., to 5 May 2027 (provided the payment is evidenced in writing).

The balance confirmation of 1 August 2024 is a written acknowledgment under section 18 made within the extended period; an email can qualify as a signed acknowledgment if authenticated, giving a fresh period till 1 August 2027.
A suit filed in December 2026 is therefore within limitation.

ABC Ltd should keep evidence of the payment entry and the authenticity of the email; as a commercial dispute, it must also comply with section 12A pre-institution mediation, where time spent in mediation is excluded.

notes.note: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law, governs domestic and international commercial arbitration and enforcement of foreign awards. Section 7 requires a written arbitration agreement, which may be in a document, emails or other electronic communication. Section 8 obliges a judicial authority to refer parties to arbitration where a valid agreement exists, and section 9 allows courts to grant interim measures before, during or after the proceedings (before enforcement); section 5 limits judicial intervention to what the Act permits.

Parties are free to agree on the number of arbitrators, which must not be even (section 10), and the appointment procedure (section 11); if they fail, the Supreme Court (international) or High Court (domestic) or a designated institution appoints. An arbitrator must disclose circumstances casting doubt on independence or impartiality (section 12, with the Fifth and Seventh Schedules), and a person in a Seventh Schedule relationship is ineligible unless the parties waive this in writing after the dispute arises. Under section 16 (kompetenz-kompetenz), the tribunal can rule on its own jurisdiction.

Under section 29A, an award in domestic arbitration must be made within 12 months from completion of pleadings, extendable by six months by consent, and further only by the court. An award can be challenged only under section 34 within three months (extendable by 30 days for sufficient cause) on limited grounds such as incapacity, invalid agreement, lack of proper notice, matters beyond the reference, improper composition, non-arbitrability, conflict with public policy and, for domestic awards, patent illegality. Once the challenge period lapses or the challenge fails, the award is enforced as a decree under section 36; filing a challenge does not automatically stay it.

Conciliation under Part III of the 1996 Act is a voluntary process where a conciliator helps parties reach a settlement; the conciliator has no power to impose a decision. A settlement agreement signed by the parties has the same status and effect as an arbitral award on agreed terms (sections 73-74). Statements made in conciliation are confidential and cannot be relied on in later arbitration or court proceedings (section 81).

The Mediation Act 2023 provides for voluntary pre-litigation mediation, to be completed within 120 days, extendable by up to 60 days. A mediated settlement agreement signed by the parties and authenticated by the mediator is final and binding and enforceable like a court judgment, and can be challenged only on limited grounds such as fraud, corruption, impersonation or non-mediable matters. It also provides for online mediation and community mediation and sets up the Mediation Council of India; the Act's provisions are being brought into force in phases, so check the notified status before the exam.

quiz.q: A supply contract has an arbitration clause. One party files a civil suit for damages, and the other applies under section 8 before submitting its first statement on the substance. The court should:
options: Try the suit since civil courts have plenary jurisdiction
Stay the suit for one year
Ask the plaintiff to elect a remedy
Refer the parties to arbitration unless prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists
quiz.explain: Section 8 mandates reference to arbitration where a valid agreement exists.

quiz.q: A contract names the employer's own Managing Director as sole arbitrator. Under the 1996 Act as amended, the appointment is:
options: Valid, as the parties agreed to it
Valid if the MD is a qualified lawyer
Invalid, as the MD is ineligible under section 12(5) unless expressly waived in writing after the dispute arises
Valid only for claims below ₹1 crore
quiz.explain: Section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule renders such persons ineligible (TRF Ltd; Perkins Eastman).

quiz.q: A party receives a domestic award on 1 January and files a section 34 challenge on 25 April, showing sufficient cause for the delay. The court:
options: Can condone delay up to 30 days beyond three months
Can condone any delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act
Must dismiss it, as the period is fixed at 60 days
Must refer it to the tribunal
quiz.explain: Section 34(3) allows three months plus a further 30 days for sufficient cause, and not beyond.

quiz.q: A party challenging an award under section 34 asks the court to treat the challenge as an automatic stay of enforcement. The correct position is:
options: Filing a challenge automatically stays the award
The award is stayed only if the tribunal agrees
Enforcement is stayed for six months
Filing alone does not stay the award; a separate application and order of the court are required
quiz.explain: Section 36(2)-(3) as amended requires a separate application and a court order for stay.

quiz.q: During conciliation, a company admits that its product had a design defect. Conciliation fails and the matter goes to arbitration. The other party wants to rely on that admission. It:
options: Cannot rely on it, as statements in conciliation are confidential and inadmissible
Can rely on it as an admission
Can rely on it with the conciliator's consent
Can rely on it only if recorded in writing
quiz.explain: Section 81 bars reliance on views and admissions made during conciliation.

quiz.q: Parties settle a dispute through mediation under the Mediation Act 2023, and the settlement is signed and authenticated by the mediator. One party later refuses to comply. The other party can:
options: Only file a fresh civil suit
Refer it to arbitration
Enforce the mediated settlement agreement like a court judgment
Claim only nominal damages
quiz.explain: A mediated settlement agreement under the Mediation Act 2023 is binding and enforceable in the same manner as a judgment or decree.

desc.q: P Ltd and Q Ltd have an arbitration clause in their contract. After a dispute, Q Ltd fears that P Ltd will sell off the disputed machinery before arbitration starts. The arbitral tribunal is not yet constituted. Advise Q Ltd on interim relief and how its position changes once the tribunal is constituted.
points: Before the tribunal is constituted, Q Ltd can apply to the court under section 9 for interim measures, such as an injunction against sale or preservation of the machinery.
If the court grants interim relief before arbitration begins, arbitral proceedings must start within 90 days (section 9(2)).
Once the tribunal is constituted, the court should not ordinarily entertain a section 9 application unless the remedy under section 17 is not efficacious (section 9(3)).
The tribunal can grant similar interim measures under section 17, and its orders are enforceable as orders of the court.
Q Ltd should also ensure a written notice invoking arbitration (section 21) and begin the appointment of arbitrators under the agreed procedure or section 11.

notes.note: Under the Indian Stamp Act 1899, an 'instrument' (section 2(14)) is any document by which a right or liability is created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished or recorded. Other key terms include 'executed' (signed), 'conveyance' (section 2(10), covering transfers of property inter vivos), 'chargeable' (as per the law in force when the instrument is executed) and 'duly stamped' (stamped with the correct amount and in the right manner). Example: a share transfer deed and a lease deed are both instruments.

Section 3 makes instruments listed in Schedule I chargeable with duty, and States prescribe their own rates for many instruments under their Stamp Acts (List II, Entry 63; rates on bills of exchange, cheques, share transfers etc. are fixed by the Union under List I, Entry 91). Under section 4, where several instruments complete one transaction, only the principal instrument bears full duty, and section 5 requires an instrument covering several distinct matters to be stamped for each. Since the Finance Act 2019, stamp duty on securities transactions is collected centrally through stock exchanges and depositories.

Instruments executed in India must be stamped before or at the time of execution (section 17), while those executed outside India may be stamped within three months of first being received in India (section 18). Duty may be paid by impressed stamps, adhesive stamps, franking or e-stamping, and adhesive stamps must be cancelled so they cannot be reused (section 12). Example: a lease deed signed today in Kerala must be on e-stamp paper bought on or before today.

Under section 35, an instrument not duly stamped is inadmissible in evidence and cannot be acted upon, but (except for a mere copy) it can be admitted on payment of the deficit duty and a penalty of ₹5 or ten times the deficit, whichever is more. Section 33 empowers authorities to impound such instruments. In the 2023 seven-judge decision on interplay of the Stamp Act and arbitration, the Supreme Court held that an unstamped agreement is not void and its arbitration clause can still be acted on, as stamping is a curable defect.

Allowance or refund is available for spoiled stamps, such as stamp paper damaged or not used for the intended purpose, on application to the Collector generally within six months (section 49 onwards). Refunds are also allowed for stamps used for an instrument found void from the start or that failed for a reason like refusal by a party, subject to deduction of a small percentage. Example: e-stamp paper bought for an agreement that the parties later cancel before signing can be refunded on timely application.

E-stamping is a computer-based system, administered in many States through the Stock Holding Corporation of India (SHCIL) as Central Record-Keeping Agency, for paying stamp duty electronically. Each certificate has a unique identification number that can be verified online, which helps prevent fake stamp papers. Most States have now replaced physical stamp paper above specified values with e-stamping.

Under section 31, a person can apply to the Collector, before or after execution, for an opinion on the duty with which an instrument is chargeable, paying a fee. The Collector issues an endorsement certificate under section 32, after which the instrument is treated as duly stamped and admissible. This is useful for complex documents such as amalgamation schemes where the applicable article is unclear.

quiz.q: An agreement executed in Bengaluru on 1 March is stamped on 10 March. The instrument is:
options: Duly stamped, since there is a one-month grace period
Not duly stamped, as instruments executed in India must be stamped before or at the time of execution
Valid only if registered
Duly stamped if adhesive stamps were used
quiz.explain: Section 17 requires stamping before or at the time of execution for instruments executed in India.

quiz.q: An unstamped loan agreement is produced in court. The court will:
options: Reject it permanently
Treat the loan as void
Admit it on payment of deficit duty and penalty
Admit it free of cost
quiz.explain: Section 35 proviso allows admission on payment of duty plus penalty.

quiz.q: A sale of land is completed through an agreement, a conveyance deed and a power of attorney, all for one transaction. Full duty is payable on:
options: Each of the three documents
None, if the price is below ₹10 lakh
Only the agreement
The principal instrument only, with others at a reduced rate
quiz.explain: Section 4 provides that only the principal instrument is charged full duty where several instruments are used for one transaction.

quiz.q: A party wants certainty about the duty payable on a complex merger scheme before filing it. He should:
options: Seek adjudication from the Collector under section 31
File a writ petition
Pay the minimum duty
Apply to the Registrar of Companies
quiz.explain: Section 31 provides for adjudication of the proper stamp duty by the Collector.

quiz.q: A company's agreement containing an arbitration clause is unstamped. Under the Supreme Court's seven-judge ruling of 2023, the arbitration clause:
options: Is void
Can be acted on only after a civil suit
Must be re-executed
Is not void; the stamp defect is curable and does not bar appointment of an arbitrator
quiz.explain: The 2023 decision held non-stamping a curable defect not rendering the agreement void.

quiz.q: A person buys e-stamp paper for a lease, but the landlord backs out before signing. To get a refund he must:
options: Apply to the High Court
File a civil suit
Apply to the Collector for allowance for spoiled stamps within the prescribed time
Sell it to another person
quiz.explain: The Act allows refunds for unused or spoiled stamps on timely application to the Collector.

desc.q: A share purchase agreement signed in Singapore between an Indian company and a foreign investor is brought to India two months later and is now needed as evidence in a Mumbai court. It is not stamped. Advise on stamp duty compliance and the agreement's admissibility.
points: An instrument executed outside India may be stamped within three months of its first receipt in India (section 18), so the company can still stamp it within that window without penalty.
The applicable rate will be under the State law where the instrument is received (Maharashtra Stamp Act), as stamp duty on many instruments is a State subject.
If it is produced in court unstamped, the court will impound it under section 33 and admit it only after payment of deficit duty and penalty (section 35).
Where the correct article is unclear, the company may seek adjudication under section 31 to obtain a certificate that the instrument is duly stamped.
An unstamped agreement is not void; the defect is curable, so commercial rights and any arbitration clause survive once duty is paid.

notes.note: Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908 makes registration compulsory for gifts of immovable property, non-testamentary instruments creating or extinguishing any interest of ₹100 or more in immovable property, leases from year to year or for more than a year, and (since 2001) agreements for sale under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 18 lists documents where registration is optional, such as wills and instruments creating interests below ₹100. Documents must be presented within four months of execution (section 23), with a further four months allowed on fine.

Under section 49, an unregistered document that requires registration does not affect the immovable property it covers and is not admissible as evidence of the transaction. It may, however, be admitted as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance or of a collateral transaction not requiring registration. Under section 47, a registered document operates from the date of its execution, not its registration; example: an unregistered sale deed does not pass title even if the price is paid.

The Transfer of Property Act 1882 (TPA) governs transfers between living persons (section 5), and any property may be transferred except those listed in section 6, such as a mere chance of inheritance (spes successionis) or a right to sue.
