A condition absolutely restraining alienation is void (section 10), and section 41 protects a transferee from an ostensible owner who took reasonable care. Under section 52 (lis pendens), a transfer of property in dispute during a suit is subject to the court's decision, and section 53A protects a buyer in possession under a written contract under the doctrine of part performance.

A sale (section 54 TPA) is a transfer of ownership for a price; for tangible immovable property worth ₹100 or more it must be by registered instrument. A mortgage (section 58) is transfer of an interest in specific immovable property to secure a loan, in forms such as simple, usufructuary, English and mortgage by deposit of title deeds (equitable mortgage, common for bank loans). A lease (section 105) transfers a right to enjoy property for a term against rent, and a gift (section 122) is a voluntary transfer without consideration, accepted during the donor's lifetime, and for immovable property must be by registered instrument attested by two witnesses (section 123).

Under the Indian Easements Act 1882, an easement is a right held by the owner of a dominant property over a servient property owned by another, for its beneficial enjoyment, such as a right of way, light or air. Easements can be acquired by grant, necessity (e.g., the only access route to landlocked land), quasi-easement, custom or prescription after 20 years' peaceable and open enjoyment as of right (section 15). An easement of necessity ends when the necessity ends, and a licence, unlike an easement, is a personal permission that creates no interest in the property.

quiz.q: A father gifts a plot to his daughter by a written deed signed by two witnesses, but it is not registered. The gift is:
options: Not effective, as a gift of immovable property must be by registered instrument
Valid, since gifts within family need no formalities
Valid if the daughter takes possession
Valid if stamp duty is paid
quiz.explain: Section 123 TPA and section 17 Registration Act require a registered instrument for gifts of immovable property.

quiz.q: During the pendency of a partition suit, one co-owner sells his share to a third party. The buyer's rights are:
options: Absolute and unaffected by the suit
Void ab initio
Subject to the final decree in the suit under the doctrine of lis pendens
Valid only if the court approves in advance
quiz.explain: Section 52 TPA makes transfers during pending litigation subject to the court's decision.

quiz.q: A borrower gives his title deeds to a bank in Mumbai with intent to create security for a loan. This creates:
options: A mortgage by deposit of title deeds
A pledge
A lease
A gift
quiz.explain: Section 58(f) TPA recognises equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds in notified towns.

quiz.q: A has used a footpath across B's land openly and as of right for 22 years without interruption. A has likely acquired:
options: A licence
Ownership of the path
A lease
An easement by prescription
quiz.explain: Section 15 of the Easements Act grants an easement after 20 years of peaceable, open and uninterrupted enjoyment as of right.

quiz.q: A five-year lease of a shop is written on stamp paper but not registered. In a dispute, the lease deed:
options: Is fully enforceable
Cannot be used to prove the lease terms, but may be used for collateral purposes
Is void and the tenant must vacate immediately
Converts into a gift
quiz.explain: Section 49 bars use of an unregistered compulsorily registrable document to prove the transaction, except for collateral purposes.

quiz.q: A agrees in writing to sell a flat to B, B takes possession and pays part of the price, but A refuses to execute the sale deed and sues to evict B. B can best rely on:
options: Section 6 TPA
Easement of necessity
Section 10 TPA
Doctrine of part performance under section 53A TPA, provided the agreement is registered
quiz.explain: Section 53A protects a transferee in possession under a written (now registered) contract who has performed or is willing to perform.

desc.q: R purchased land under a registered sale deed. Later he learns that (i) the seller had earlier mortgaged it to a bank by deposit of title deeds, and (ii) a neighbour claims a right of way over it, used for 25 years. Advise R on his position.
points: A sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more requires a registered deed (section 54 TPA); R's registered deed gives him title from the date of execution (section 47 Registration Act).
An equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds (section 58(f) TPA) is valid even without a registered document, so R takes the land subject to the bank's prior charge.
R should check encumbrance records and may claim against the seller for breach of the implied covenant that the property is free from undisclosed encumbrances (section 55 TPA).
If the neighbour proves 20 years' open, peaceful and uninterrupted use as of right, he has a prescriptive easement (section 15 Easements Act) binding on R as owner of the servient land.
R cannot block the path but may challenge the claim if the use was by permission (a licence) or was interrupted.

notes.note: Under section 2(f) of the Right to Information Act 2005, 'information' means any material in any form, including records, documents, emails, opinions, contracts, samples and electronic data, as well as information about a private body that a public authority can access under any law. 'Right to information' (section 2(j)) includes inspecting records, taking notes and certified copies and obtaining samples. A citizen applies under section 6 without giving reasons, and the Public Information Officer (PIO) must reply within 30 days, or 48 hours where life or liberty is involved (section 7).

A public authority (section 2(h)) is any body constituted by or under the Constitution, a law of Parliament or a State legislature, or a government notification, including bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed by government, and NGOs substantially financed by government. Each must suo motu publish key information about its functions, officers and budgets (section 4) and appoint PIOs. Section 8 exempts certain information, such as information affecting national security, commercial confidence, cabinet papers and unwarranted invasion of privacy, unless larger public interest requires disclosure; example: a private listed company is not a public authority, but its filings held by a regulator can be sought from that regulator.

The Central Information Commission (CIC) and State Information Commissions (SICs) are set up under sections 12 and 15, with a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners each. After a first appeal to the senior officer within the authority (section 19(1), within 30 days), a second appeal lies to the Commission within 90 days, and complaints may be filed directly under section 18. Under section 20, the Commission can impose a penalty of ₹250 per day, up to ₹25,000, on a PIO who refuses or delays information without reasonable cause; since the 2019 amendment, the tenure and salaries of Commissioners are as prescribed by the Central Government.

quiz.q: A citizen files an RTI application seeking information on the custodial detention of his brother, which affects his liberty. The PIO must respond within:
options: 48 hours
30 days
15 days
7 days
quiz.explain: Section 7(1) proviso requires a reply within 48 hours where life or liberty is concerned.

quiz.q: A PIO asks an applicant to state why he wants copies of tender files before supplying them. This demand is:
options: Valid, as reasons help prioritise
Valid for commercial information
Improper, as an applicant need not give reasons for seeking information
Valid only for foreign nationals
quiz.explain: Section 6(2) states that the applicant is not required to give any reason.

quiz.q: A private school receiving no government funds is asked under RTI for its fee records. The school:
options: Is not a public authority, but information about it held by the Education Department can be sought from that department
Must give the information directly
Is a public authority as it provides education
Can be penalised by the CIC
quiz.explain: Only bodies within section 2(h) are public authorities; section 2(f) covers private-body information accessible to a public authority.

quiz.q: An applicant gets no reply from the PIO within 30 days and his first appeal is also not decided. His next step is:
options: A writ petition under Article 32 only
A civil suit
A complaint to the police
A second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days
quiz.explain: Section 19(3) provides a second appeal to the CIC/SIC within 90 days.

quiz.q: The Commission finds a PIO delayed information for 150 days without reasonable cause. The maximum penalty it can impose is:
quiz.explain: Section 20(1) prescribes ₹250 per day subject to a maximum of ₹25,000.

quiz.q: A competitor seeks a company's detailed bid pricing submitted to a ministry. The ministry can refuse because:
options: Companies have no rights under RTI
The information is protected as commercial confidence under section 8(1)(d), unless larger public interest warrants disclosure
Tenders are classified as state secrets
Only the CAG can access tender files
quiz.explain: Section 8(1)(d) exempts trade secrets and commercial confidence that would harm competitive position.

desc.q: A shareholder of a listed company seeks, under the RTI Act, (i) the company's internal board minutes directly from the company and (ii) inspection reports about the company held by SEBI. Advise on the likely outcome of each request.
points: A listed private company is not a 'public authority' under section 2(h), so the request made directly to the company is not maintainable under the RTI Act.
SEBI is a statutory body and a public authority, so a request for information held by it is maintainable.

SEBI may invoke exemptions under section 8, such as commercial confidence, information held in a fiduciary relationship, or information that would impede investigation, unless larger public interest warrants disclosure.
Where only part of the information is exempt, the PIO should disclose the non-exempt portion through severability (section 10).
If refused, the shareholder may file a first appeal within 30 days and a second appeal to the CIC within 90 days; he may also use his rights under company law to inspect statutory records.

notes.note: The Information Technology Act 2000 gives legal recognition to electronic records and transactions. Key definitions in section 2 include 'electronic record', 'computer resource', 'intermediary' (any person who receives, stores or transmits records on behalf of others, such as ISPs, marketplaces and social media platforms) and 'addressee' and 'originator'. Sections 4 and 5 recognise electronic records and electronic signatures where law requires writing or signature, but section 1(4) and the First Schedule exclude documents such as wills, powers of attorney, trusts and contracts for sale of immovable property.

A digital signature (section 3) authenticates an electronic record using an asymmetric crypto system and hash function, with a private key to sign and a public key to verify. Section 3A recognises other reliable electronic signature techniques notified in the Second Schedule, such as Aadhaar-based e-sign. Example: directors sign MCA filings with a Digital Signature Certificate (DSC), and the recipient can verify both the signer's identity and that the document has not been altered.

The Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) licenses and regulates Certifying Authorities (sections 17-34) and maintains the root certifying authority. A Certifying Authority issues Digital Signature Certificates after verifying the applicant's identity, and must follow secure procedures and publish its practices. It may suspend or revoke a certificate on the subscriber's request or if it was obtained by misrepresentation or the key is compromised (sections 37-38).

Section 43 makes a person who accesses, downloads, introduces viruses into or damages a computer system without permission liable to pay compensation, adjudicated by an Adjudicating Officer (section 46). Criminal offences include tampering with source code (section 65), dishonest or fraudulent acts under section 43 (section 66), identity theft (section 66C), cheating by personation using a computer (section 66D), privacy violation (section 66E), cyber-terrorism (section 66F) and publishing obscene material electronically (section 67). Section 66A was struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015), and section 85 makes officers in charge liable for offences by companies unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence.

Section 43A, read with the 2011 SPDI Rules, made a body corporate handling 'sensitive personal data or information' (passwords, financial data, health records, biometric data, sexual orientation, etc.) liable to compensate for negligent failure to maintain reasonable security practices. Section 72A punishes disclosure of personal information in breach of a lawful contract. Once the relevant provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 are in force, section 43A is omitted and the DPDP regime governs.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act) governs processing of digital personal data, which must be on a lawful ground, chiefly consent or certain 'legitimate uses'. Data fiduciaries must give notice, ensure accuracy and security, report breaches and erase data when the purpose is served, while data principals have rights of access, correction, erasure and grievance redress; processing children's data needs verifiable parental consent. The Data Protection Board of India adjudicates breaches and can impose penalties up to ₹250 crore per instance, and the DPDP Rules 2025 phase in its obligations; example: an e-commerce company must stop processing a customer's data once consent is withdrawn.

quiz.q: A party argues that a will executed and signed electronically with a DSC is valid under the IT Act. The correct position is:
options: Valid, as the IT Act recognises all electronic records
Valid if stored on a government server
Valid if notarised online
Not valid, as wills are excluded from the IT Act by the First Schedule
quiz.explain: Section 1(4) and the First Schedule exclude testamentary dispositions such as wills.

quiz.q: A person logs in to his former employer's server with an old password and downloads client data to sell to a rival. He is liable for:
options: Only civil compensation under section 43
Only defamation
Compensation under section 43 and, as he acted dishonestly, an offence under section 66
No liability, since he knew the password
quiz.explain: Unauthorised access and download is covered by section 43, and doing it dishonestly or fraudulently is an offence under section 66.

quiz.q: A fraudster creates a fake social media profile of a bank officer and induces customers to share OTPs. The specific offence is:
options: Cheating by personation using a computer resource under section 66D
Tampering with source code under section 65
Publishing obscene material under section 67
Cyber-terrorism under section 66F
quiz.explain: Section 66D punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource.

quiz.q: Who grants licences to Certifying Authorities to issue Digital Signature Certificates in India?
options: RBI
CERT-In
MCA
Controller of Certifying Authorities
quiz.explain: Sections 17-24 of the IT Act empower the Controller to license and regulate Certifying Authorities.

quiz.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, a fintech app wants to process a 15-year-old's personal data for a student account. It must:
options: Obtain verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian
Obtain the child's consent alone
Notify the Data Protection Board first
Get CERT-In approval
quiz.explain: The DPDP Act requires verifiable parental consent for processing a child's (under 18) personal data.

quiz.q: A company's IT Head knew about repeated security lapses that led to a cyber offence by the company but did nothing. Under section 85 of the IT Act, he:
options: Can never be prosecuted, as only the company is liable
Is liable only if he personally committed the act
Can be deemed guilty, unless he proves the offence was without his knowledge or he exercised due diligence
Is liable only to pay a fine to the company
quiz.explain: Section 85 makes persons in charge liable unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence.

desc.q: An online retailer suffers a data breach exposing customers' card details and passwords due to an unpatched server. Customers complain and the retailer's board seeks advice. Discuss the legal consequences under the IT Act 2000 and the DPDP Act 2023.
points: Card details and passwords are sensitive personal data; under section 43A (while in force) the retailer is liable to pay compensation for negligent failure to maintain reasonable security practices.
Under the DPDP Act, the retailer as data fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards, and must notify the Data Protection Board and affected data principals of the breach.
The Board can impose heavy penalties (up to ₹250 crore for failure to take reasonable security safeguards), considering the gravity and mitigation steps.
The retailer must also report the cyber incident to CERT-In within the prescribed timeline under its directions.
Officers in charge may face liability under section 85 for offences by the company; the board should fix vulnerabilities, document due diligence and offer remedial support to customers.

notes.note: Under the Indian Contract Act 1872 (ICA), a proposal (section 2(a)) becomes a promise when accepted, and acceptance must be absolute and unqualified (section 7); a counter-offer rejects the original offer. Communication of an offer is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree, and of acceptance as against the proposer when put in the course of transmission to him (section 4). An invitation to treat, such as goods displayed with price tags or a catalogue, is not an offer; general offers to the public can be accepted by performing the conditions (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co; Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt, where knowledge of the offer was required).

Consideration (section 2(d)) is an act, abstinence or promise done at the desire of the promisor by the promisee or any other person, and may be past, present or future. It need not be adequate, but must be real and lawful; under section 25, an agreement without consideration is void, except a registered written promise made out of natural love and affection, a promise to compensate for something voluntarily done, and a written promise to pay a time-barred debt. Example: a promise by a son to pay a contractor for repairs his father requested earlier is enforceable as past consideration at the promisor's desire.

Only a party to a contract can sue on it (Tweddle v Atkinson; Dunlop v Selfridge), though in India consideration may flow from a third person (Chinnaya v Ramayya). Exceptions include beneficiaries of a trust or charge, family settlements and marriage arrangements, acknowledgment or estoppel, and covenants running with land. Example: a beneficiary under an insurance policy trust can enforce the policy even though not a party.

Under section 11, a person is competent to contract if he has attained majority (18 years), is of sound mind and is not disqualified by law. An agreement with a minor is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, 1903), cannot be ratified on attaining majority, and the minor is not estopped by misrepresenting his age, but a minor's property is liable for necessaries supplied to him (section 68). A person who is usually of unsound mind may contract when of sound mind (section 12), and vice versa.

Consent is free when not caused by coercion (section 15), undue influence (section 16), fraud (section 17), misrepresentation (section 18) or mistake. Contracts caused by the first four are voidable at the option of the aggrieved party (sections 19-19A), while a bilateral mistake of fact essential to the agreement makes it void (section 20); a mistake of Indian law does not (section 21). Example: an agreement signed at gunpoint is voidable for coercion, and silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak.

A void agreement (section 2(g)) is not enforceable at all, e.g., agreements in restraint of trade (section 27, subject to the exception for sale of goodwill), in restraint of legal proceedings (section 28), uncertain agreements (section 29) and wagers (section 30). A voidable contract (section 2(i)) is enforceable at the option of one party, as in a contract induced by fraud. A contract that becomes void later, for example through impossibility, requires any advantage received to be restored under section 65; an employee's post-employment non-compete clause is generally void in India.

A contract may be discharged by performance, mutual agreement (novation, rescission, alteration, remission, waiver under section 62-63), impossibility, lapse of time, operation of law or breach. Under section 56, a contract becomes void when performance becomes impossible or unlawful after it is made (frustration), as when the subject matter is destroyed, though mere commercial hardship or rise in cost is not frustration (Satyabrata Ghose, 1954). Example: a hall booked for a wedding burns down before the date, so the contract is discharged.

On breach, section 73 entitles the injured party to compensation for loss arising naturally in the usual course of things or which the parties knew, when contracting, to be likely to result (Hadley v Baxendale); remote and indirect losses are not recoverable. Under section 74, where a sum is named as liquidated damages or penalty, only reasonable compensation up to that amount is awarded (Kailash Nath Associates, 2015). Other remedies include rescission, quantum meruit for work done, specific performance and injunctions; the injured party must also take reasonable steps to mitigate loss.

Quasi-contracts (sections 68-72) impose obligations without an agreement to prevent unjust enrichment. They cover necessaries supplied to an incapable person (section 68), payment by an interested person of money due by another (section 69), non-gratuitous acts whose benefit is enjoyed (section 70), finder of goods (section 71) and money paid or goods delivered by mistake or coercion (section 72). Example: if a company mistakenly pays an invoice twice, the supplier must return the excess under section 72.

E-contracts formed through emails, websites, click-wrap and shrink-wrap agreements are valid if they satisfy the usual essentials of the ICA, and section 10A of the IT Act expressly recognises contracts formed electronically. Rules on time and place of dispatch and receipt of electronic records are in section 13 of the IT Act, typically the place of business of the originator and addressee. Courts have upheld clicking 'I agree' as acceptance, though unfair standard terms may be scrutinised; example: an online booking confirmation email completes the contract.

quiz.q: A shop displays a phone tagged '₹20,000'. A customer offers ₹20,000 but the shopkeeper refuses to sell. The customer:
options: Can enforce a contract, as the price tag was an offer
Cannot enforce it, as a display of goods is only an invitation to treat
Can claim damages for refusal
Can file a consumer complaint for breach of contract
quiz.explain: Display of goods with prices is an invitation to offer; the customer makes the offer.

quiz.q: A 17-year-old takes a loan of ₹2 lakh by falsely claiming to be 19 and signs a mortgage. The lender sues to recover. The court will hold:
options: The minor is liable as he lied
The contract is valid on attaining majority
The agreement is void, and the minor is not estopped by his false statement
The minor's parents are liable
quiz.explain: Mohori Bibee holds minors' agreements void ab initio, and estoppel does not apply against a minor.

quiz.q: A writes to B: 'I will sell my car for ₹5 lakh.' B replies: 'I accept, if you include new tyres.' A sells to C. B sues. B will:
options: Succeed, as he accepted
Succeed if he pays more
Succeed only for damages
Fail, since his reply was a counter-offer and not an absolute acceptance
quiz.explain: Section 7 requires absolute and unqualified acceptance; a conditional reply is a counter-offer.

quiz.q: A supplier fails to deliver a machine part on time. The buyer's factory stays shut and loses a special export order the supplier did not know about. The buyer can recover:
options: Normal losses arising from the delay, but not the loss of the special export order
All losses including the export order
Only nominal damages
Nothing, since delay is not breach
quiz.explain: Section 73 and Hadley v Baxendale exclude losses not within the parties' contemplation.

quiz.q: A contract provides liquidated damages of ₹10 lakh for delay. The delay causes actual loss of ₹3 lakh. The court is likely to award:
options: ₹10 lakh automatically
Nothing
₹13 lakh
Reasonable compensation not exceeding ₹10 lakh, around the proven loss of ₹3 lakh
quiz.explain: Section 74 limits recovery to reasonable compensation up to the stipulated sum.

quiz.q: A courier mistakenly delivers goods meant for X to Y, who uses them knowing they were not ordered. Y is liable to pay because:
options: Of section 70 of the ICA
Of section 27
He was negligent in tort
Of section 56
quiz.explain: Section 70 makes a person who enjoys the benefit of a non-gratuitous act liable to compensate.

desc.q: TechCo agrees to develop software for RetailCo for ₹40 lakh by 31 March. In February, new government regulations ban the specific payment feature that was the core of the software. Separately, TechCo's key developer resigns, raising its costs by 30%. RetailCo wants to cancel and recover the ₹10 lakh advance. Advise both parties.
points: Under section 56, a contract becomes void if performance becomes unlawful or impossible after it is made; a regulatory ban on the core feature may frustrate the contract to that extent.
Increased cost or loss of a key developer is mere commercial hardship and does not frustrate the contract (Satyabrata Ghose).
If the contract is frustrated, section 65 requires TechCo to restore the advantage received, i.e., refund the advance, though it may claim for work done that benefited RetailCo.
If only part is affected, the parties may vary the scope by mutual agreement (section 62) rather than cancel.
If RetailCo cancels without legal ground, TechCo can claim damages under section 73, and must mitigate its losses.

notes.note: Under section 4 of the Sale of Goods Act 1930, a contract of sale is one by which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer property in goods to the buyer for a price. Essentials are two parties, movable goods (including shares, growing crops and stock, but not actionable claims or money), a money price, transfer of general property, and the usual essentials of a valid contract. Example: exchange of goods for goods is barter, not sale.

Where property passes to the buyer immediately, it is a sale; where it is to pass at a future time or on a condition, it is an agreement to sell, which becomes a sale when that time arrives or the condition is met. In a sale, risk generally passes with property (section 26), so loss falls on the buyer, and the seller can sue for price (section 55); in an agreement to sell, the seller bears risk and can sue only for damages. Example: if a car sold is destroyed by fire before delivery but after property has passed, the buyer bears the loss.

A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract whose breach allows repudiation, while a warranty is collateral and its breach only gives a right to damages (section 12). Implied conditions include title (section 14), description (section 15), fitness for purpose and merchantable quality (section 16), and sale by sample (section 17); implied warranties include quiet possession and freedom from encumbrances. Under section 13, a buyer may waive a breach of condition and treat it as a breach of warranty, and must do so once he has accepted the goods.

Under section 16, there is no implied condition as to quality or fitness, so the buyer must take care when buying ('let the buyer beware'). Exceptions include where the buyer makes known a particular purpose and relies on the seller's skill, goods bought by description from a dealer (merchantable quality), sale by sample, usage of trade and where the seller uses fraud. Example: a buyer who tells a dealer he needs paint for marine use and relies on his advice can reject paint unfit for that purpose (Priest v Last).

An unpaid seller (section 45) is one who has not been paid in full or has received a dishonoured negotiable instrument. Against the goods he has a lien while in possession (sections 47-49), a right of stoppage in transit if the buyer becomes insolvent (sections 50-52), and a right of resale in specified cases (section 54). He also has rights against the buyer personally: a suit for price (section 55), damages for non-acceptance (section 56) and interest.

quiz.q: A agrees to sell B 100 bags of rice from his godown, to be weighed and set apart next week. Before that, the godown is flooded. The loss falls on:
options: A, as property had not passed and this was an agreement to sell
B, since the contract was made
Both equally
The insurer only
quiz.explain: Property in unascertained goods passes only when ascertained; risk follows property (section 26).

quiz.q: A buyer tells a dealer he needs a pump to lift water 50 metres and relies on the dealer's choice. The pump cannot lift beyond 20 metres. The buyer can:
options: Only claim damages
Reject the pump for breach of implied condition of fitness for purpose
Do nothing due to caveat emptor
Sue only the manufacturer
quiz.explain: Section 16(1) implies a condition of fitness where the buyer discloses the purpose and relies on the seller's skill.

quiz.q: A buyer purchases a stolen car from a person with no title, and the true owner reclaims it. The buyer can recover the price from the seller for breach of:
options: Implied warranty of quality
Caveat emptor
Section 56
Implied condition as to title under section 14
quiz.explain: Section 14 implies a condition that the seller has the right to sell.

quiz.q: A seller has handed goods to a carrier for delivery when he learns the buyer has become insolvent and has not paid. The seller can:
options: Exercise the right of stoppage in transit and resume possession
Only file a claim in insolvency
Exercise lien
Sue the carrier
quiz.explain: Sections 50-52 give an unpaid seller a right of stoppage in transit on the buyer's insolvency.

quiz.q: A buyer orders 'Basmati rice' by catalogue but receives non-Basmati rice of good quality. The buyer can:
options: Reject, because there is a breach of implied condition that goods correspond with description
Not reject, since quality is good
Only claim a price cut
Reject only if he paid in advance
quiz.explain: Section 15 implies a condition that goods correspond with their description.

quiz.q: A buyer finds a defect but keeps and uses the goods for months. He can now:
options: Reject the goods for breach of condition
Treat the breach of condition only as a breach of warranty and claim damages
Rescind the contract
Get a full refund
quiz.explain: Under section 13, once goods are accepted, a breach of condition can only be treated as a breach of warranty.

desc.q: S sold 500 kg of spices to B on credit, payable in 30 days. B took delivery of 200 kg; 300 kg are still in S's warehouse. Before payment, B's cheque bounces and S learns B is facing insolvency. Advise S on his rights as unpaid seller.
points: S is an unpaid seller under section 45, as the cheque was dishonoured and the price remains unpaid.
For the 300 kg in his possession, S can exercise a lien and retain the goods until paid, since the credit has effectively failed and B is insolvent (section 47).
Since the goods are perishable and/or after notice to B, S may resell them and claim any shortfall from B as damages (section 54).
For the 200 kg already delivered, S's rights against the goods are lost; he can only sue B for the price (section 55) and file a claim in B's insolvency proceedings.
S may also proceed under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for the dishonoured cheque.

notes.note: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 (NI Act), the parties to a bill of exchange are the drawer (who orders payment), the drawee (who is ordered to pay and becomes acceptor on acceptance) and the payee; to a promissory note, the maker and payee; and to a cheque, the drawer, the drawee bank and the payee. Further parties include the endorser and endorsee, holder (section 8), and holder in due course (section 9), who took the instrument for value, before maturity and in good faith. A holder in due course gets a title free of the defects of prior parties, and all prior parties remain liable to him until the instrument is satisfied (section 36).

Under section 87, a material alteration made without the consent of the parties, such as changing the amount, date, payee, time or place of payment, voids the instrument as against any party who did not consent. Exceptions include alterations made with consent, to carry out the common intention of the parties, filling blanks under authority (section 20), crossing a cheque or converting a blank endorsement into a full one. A bank paying an apparently unaltered cheque in due course is protected (section 89).

A crossing directs the paying bank to pay only through a bank account, not over the counter. A general crossing is two parallel lines with or without words like '& Co.' (section 123), a special crossing names a particular bank (section 124), and 'Account Payee' directs the collecting bank to credit only the payee's account; 'Not Negotiable' (section 130) means the transferee gets no better title than the transferor. A paying bank that pays contrary to crossing is liable to the true owner (section 129), while one paying in due course is protected (section 128).

Under section 138, dishonour of a cheque for insufficient funds is an offence if the cheque was issued for a legally enforceable debt, presented within its validity (three months), the payee sends a written demand notice within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour, and the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of the notice. The complaint must be filed within one month after that 15-day period (section 142), and the offence is punishable with imprisonment up to two years or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The court may order interim compensation of up to 20% (section 143A), and section 141 makes officers in charge of a company liable.

Section 118 presumes, until the contrary is proved, that every negotiable instrument was made for consideration, bears the date shown, was accepted and transferred before maturity, and that the holder is a holder in due course. Section 139 presumes that the holder of a cheque received it in discharge of a debt or liability, a rebuttable presumption that the accused can displace on a preponderance of probabilities (Rangappa v Sri Mohan, 2010; Basalingappa, 2019). Example: once the drawer admits signing the cheque, the burden shifts to him to show there was no debt.

quiz.q: A cheque crossed 'Account Payee' in favour of R is stolen and the thief tries to encash it at the counter. The bank should:
options: Pay cash, since the cheque is genuine
Refer to the police only
Pay half the amount
Refuse cash payment and credit it only to R's account
quiz.explain: A crossed cheque cannot be paid over the counter, and an account-payee crossing directs credit only to the payee.

quiz.q: After issuing a promissory note for ₹50,000, the payee alters the amount to ₹80,000 without the maker's consent. The note is:
options: Valid for ₹80,000
Valid for ₹50,000 only
Void against the maker due to material alteration
Valid if registered
quiz.explain: Section 87 renders an instrument void against a party who did not consent to a material alteration.

quiz.q: A cheque bounces on 1 March and the payee receives the bank memo on 3 March. The demand notice must be sent by:
options: 2 April
2 April counted from dishonour
15 March
Within 30 days of 3 March
quiz.explain: Section 138(b) requires notice within 30 days of receipt of information about the dishonour.

quiz.q: A director in charge of day-to-day affairs of a company that issued a dishonoured cheque is prosecuted along with the company. He can escape liability if he proves:
options: The offence was committed without his knowledge or he exercised all due diligence
He was not the signatory
He resigned after the cheque was issued
The company is solvent
quiz.explain: Section 141 allows persons in charge to escape by proving lack of knowledge or due diligence.

quiz.q: In a section 138 trial, the accused admits signing the cheque but says it was given as security, not for any debt. The legal position is:
options: The complainant must prove the debt beyond doubt
The case is automatically dismissed
The presumption under section 139 arises, and the accused must rebut it on a preponderance of probabilities
The accused must prove innocence beyond reasonable doubt
quiz.explain: Section 139 raises a rebuttable presumption of a legally enforceable debt once the cheque is admitted.

quiz.q: H receives a bill of exchange for value, before maturity and without notice of a defect in the endorser's title. H can enforce it against:
options: All prior parties, free of defects in their title, as a holder in due course
Only the last endorser
Only the drawer
No one, if the original payee was defrauded
quiz.explain: Sections 9 and 36 give a holder in due course a clear title and rights against all prior parties.

desc.q: M Ltd issued a cheque of ₹6 lakh to N for supplies. It was dishonoured for 'funds insufficient' on 10 January; N received the bank memo on 12 January, sent notice on 5 February, and M Ltd did not pay. N wants to prosecute M Ltd and its directors. Advise N on the procedure and liability.
points: Ingredients of section 138 are met: cheque for a legally enforceable debt, dishonour for insufficiency, notice within 30 days of receiving information (5 February is within 30 days of 12 January), and non-payment within 15 days.

The cause of action arises on expiry of 15 days from M Ltd's receipt of notice, and the complaint must be filed within one month thereafter (section 142), before the court where N's bank account is maintained.

M Ltd is liable as drawer; under section 141, directors in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business at the time are also liable, but the complaint must specifically aver their role, and non-executive/independent directors are generally not liable without specific allegations.
The presumption under section 139 helps N; M Ltd may rebut it by showing no debt existed.
N may seek interim compensation of up to 20% (section 143A); punishment is up to two years' imprisonment and/or fine up to twice the amount, and the offence is compoundable.
